But you said a minute ago that law and order, or the situation in the defence at the municipality, was such that the police could not carry out their tasks anymore, and that was the reason for the president of the municipality to mobilise the Territorial Defence. In other words, you're saying that the Territorial Defence was supposed to carry out policing tasks. Under what law?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I didn't say that, and I say that the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence had a legal foundation. And you are trying to put words into my mouth that are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It has been recorded, Witness, as your words, but okay. Could we please see paragraph 51 -- I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that a question? What kind of a comment is that that Dr. Karadzic is making at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, refrain from making statements. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read out to you: [In English] "I recognise the voices of Rajko Koprivica and Radovan Karadzic speaking in this conversation. I was at the meeting they are talking about in this conversation. It was the meeting of the Council of National Defence, which happened immediately after the reserve forces of the police were mobilised. I think there's an error in the transcription. On the last page of this conversation, there is the word 'pilav,' but in fact it should be 'Bilal.' It refers to Bilal Hasanovic, the president of the Vogosca Municipal Assembly. The topic of this meeting was Hasanovic's initiative to mobilise the Territorial Defence." [Interpretation] So that let's take a look further down the page, and you say: [In English] "... and Stanko Erakovic, on behalf of the Secretariat for National Defence. Elvedin Mehic eventually replaced him." [Interpretation] So to prevent Stanko Erakovic to stop you from voting this decision, you replaced him by a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'll explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, don't explain. Was Erakovic a Serb?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, please let me explain this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question was simple. Was Erakovic a Serb, and was Mehic, his deputy, a Muslim? Did he replace him at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- there's been numerous times when the witness has been asked to expand on his answers, and Dr. Karadzic has put him off for whatever reason. And he's directed a request to Your Honours now to explain further on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, whenever you find it necessary, you can -- you are entitled to respond. Please, by all means. If necessary, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm for going into private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Witness, this is a conversation of 7 September 1991. Jovan Tintor and Milan Plakalovic are talking. Could we please see page 4 of the Serbian and page 6 of the English. There was some foul language. We'll skip that. And Tintor said: "What will Hilmo do?" And then he swears: "Well, he won't appoint Serbian personnel." And Plakalovic says: "Well, he doesn't make appointments. He just doesn't allow any appointments until Petrovac, Pale, Nevesinje and Sipovo are resolved." And then there's foul language again: "It's a madhouse. They won't appoint anybody before this is resolved." Then Tintor says: "Oh, they won't, will they? We will have Vogosca now, and then all the people will go out here, all of them, 10.000 people, to block all the roads, all of them. Nobody shall move anywhere. No, Mato cannot be here with us, not even if he were God himself." And then the other says -- there's foul language, and Tintor says: "You know that it was said this way. And everything was promised, but they lied all the way." And then Plakalovic: "Well, listen, I saw Momo, and said that Mato should be pushed into the criminal section and that little Skrbic should stay as a deputy down there." Could we go to the following page in the Serbian. Tintor says: "Yes." And the next page in the English, please. We wanted to go to the following pages in both versions. In English, we need page 7. Tintor says: "There aren't even 4 per cent of them." He's referring to the Croats, because Mato is a Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Tintor meant, but I know that Mato is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And Plakalovic says -- Tintor says: "Yes, yes." And then: "The Croats, there aren't even 4 per cent of them. They can't." And we'll skip these two. And then Tintor said: "It's going to be a madhouse. We were telling them nicely, 'Don't do it, don't do it.' You know what they did to us? They had a chief. And having a chief, you know what their advantage is over us. They have 18 deputies, and we have 15." And then the other says: "Yes." And then Tintor: "Well, they won by some 600 people. Okay, never mind. You appoint number 1, we appoint number 2. You appoint number 3, we appoint number 4. You appoint number 5, no problem. Let us have a 3:2 ratio. But that is not fair either, because if they have the number one-man -- but what the hell. But they gave us the crime section, which is under the commander now. You know they were ..." And the other says: "Yeah, yeah." And Tintor says: "And now, well, we are entitled to a deputy. So, as a matter of fact, we have one man. And this one is removed ..." Let's go to the next page 8 in English. Actually, we're still on the 7th page. And it says: "Well, yes. And now, for God's sake, the remover [as interpreted] man who was working on farms, a chief ..." And this one says: "I know, I know. He was there the other day." And then there's foul language: "Now we don't have him either. Oh, God." And they remove the man, they have him retired, who was in charge of reserve forces. And: "Why, what do you know? Some Simo Vuleta guy? Do you know him?" Let's go on to page 9. Jovan Tintor says: "Well, he was sent into retirement." And then there's foul language: "We don't have one single man. They took over the whole of the but we are going to create our own SUP. It will be the first SUP in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the first for Serb SUP." And the other says, Don't pull my leg, or something of that kind. And then Tintor says: "Sure, we'll divide everything. And now go ahead and throw us out. If all the police is 100 per cent, Serbs or one side, and you guys go ahead and make yourself a SUP. No problem at all." So can you see what kind of what anger and uncertainty and tension you caused by making such arrangement -- arrangements? Have you identified this conversation?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll comment later in closed session. Could we now see 65 ter 30230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You read out the transcript for five minutes, and the question you asked is: "Have you identified this conversation?" What kind of question it was?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was for public session. To ask the right question, I need to go into private session. But I wanted to show one more and then ask the question in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 65 ter 30230.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After this, we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, we have that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was on the 12th of September, three days after that added conversation of five, the conversation between Jovan Tintor and Mico Stanisic, and we see that they are on a -- they are addressing each other formally, so they aren't even close friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have English translation? Yes, it appeared now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the following page. The third line from the top, where Tintor says: "All right." And then a tiny swear word: "Well, I just thought I would call you --" Actually, in the English we also need page 2. All right. This is line 10 in the English page: "I said to myself that I should call you. Those people of mine are not getting off my neck, and they are right. Do you know whether anyone has submitted the report about what has been done here in Vogosca?" Then they refer to this Andjelic. And then on the next page, he says: "Let me tell you this, Jovo. I, as a lawyer, have my own view." Tintor: "Yes." Stanisic: "Yes, and it's not clear to me that anyone can be appointed while the other person is not relieved of duty first. Can this be done?" Stanisic: "Well, I couldn't believe that this could be done like that, that somebody was appointed to perform a certain job and the other person was not replaced anywhere, and there was no decision replacing the person who was carrying out that duty so far."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We were not able to find the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the same thing with the deputy commander, when Stanisic says: "People really don't know. I mean, I am a person who respects the law, I do what the law says. A small cuss word, this is the only rule, according to me." Tintor says: "Yes." Stanisic: "Because everything else, as soon as you give privileges to somebody else, it has to bring some harm, and the other way around of the." Tintor: "Yes, yes." Stanisic: "As soon as you are harming one person, then you are granting privilege to another person, and that is not a normal thing for lawyers." Thank you. New Serbian page. And then Stanisic says: "And so they visited me. They know about the problem in the MUP, and I expect them to make a correction. Man, first of all, I mean, I would not want -- if I were in their place, I would not allow myself to be so illiterate and so ignorance of the judicial system ..." English 3, page 3 in the English. Tintor says: "You know what? I'll be honest with you. There is another thing more now. We were -- I was promised, Wait for two days, wait for seven days. We waited. You should know that the first SUP that will have the Serbian side and the Muslim police will be the Vogosca SUP. Remember this, what I've told you today, Minister. You are free to say that 10.000 Serbs will get out. I will take them out, and let me see the ass," the lower side of the back, "that will approach that SUP, and we will write ..." All right. Can we go to the bottom. Tintor says: "We have no other solution. We waited according to the law this and that. There is no law here. All human rights are being violated, and the issue is no longer dignity of our nation. Be sure that tonight I will raise 10.000 people, and there is no," small cuss word, "that that will pass. Get a thousand members of the special forces, but you can only take the dead out of here ... Vogosca. Remember what I have just told you. The Serb people in Vogosca will not suffer because of this injustice. This is not the case," and so on and so forth. I think that what he meant to say was that things are not even done like that in Katanga. Katanga was a symbol for uprisings and rebellion. Can we look at page 5 in English and the following page in the Serbian. Stanisic says: "Jovo, one needs to wait a little bit. We should wait for the heads to cool." Tintor says: "My head is quite cool. We have been cooling our heads long enough here in Vogosca. People are making fun of us; of the Serbian party, too. The things they're doing to us, they're slowly kicking our people out." And then a cuss word: "They have no solutions, other people get the solutions, and these did not get it. People are standing, they are throwing away their -- they are tearing off the doors, desks. There is nothing like that in this entire world." And then it's at the bottom of the Serbian on this page and page 6 in the English. Stanisic says: "I have to admit one thing, because I always try to be objective. The way it happened is not the way it should have happened. I still have not sorted out things for myself. Maybe the people who are at the top of the MUP do not know that it was done in this manner, because," cuss word, "it depends on how the chief or certain persons presented it, you know, and everyone has his own way. Well, Jovo, let me check it out. I will call Vito now. I will call Momo too ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This exhibit is already in evidence. Let him read, and you can ask questions. You read out for seven minutes now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But for the record, I have to note the intercept we looked at was 65 ter 30230, which was admitted as Exhibit P2219. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 12 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to reformulate this question. Are you aware that in such multi-ethnic communities, the distribution and the balance of posts is a sensitive matter, and that in our case, it was something that was done at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that balance among the ethnic groups is a sensitive and necessary thing. And what we did in Vogosca was done solely and exclusively in accordance with the law, in accordance with the census from 1991, and in accordance with professional standards, which are very important. I don't know why you are trying to present that as a replacing of the Serbian personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who authorised you to make these changes and to alter the republican agreement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not change the republican agreement. I didn't need any kind of authorisation in order to act in a professional manner. I did not change the republican agreement. The SDS and the SDA agreed to balance the national structure according to the census from 1991. Does that constitute a change?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, that is not correct. The balance was agreed on by having agreement on which post belongs to which people. You said yourself that some Muslims were replaced, Kemal Sabovic, Jasarevic and others, and when a Muslim is replaced, a Muslim comes instead of him, and you changed that in your area at a sensitive time and in a sensitive area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: There's no question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it wasn't translated. I did say:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean causing the civil war, I think that your assertion absolutely does not stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if you're thinking of the need to respect the inter-party agreement, and for the national structure of employees in national organs reflects the census from 1991, I didn't do anything else but that. If that is something that is bothering you, then that is your problem, it's not my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are changing the tracks. It wasn't like that. Can we please look at 65 ter 30267. You identified this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The 65 ter number again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 30267. I think that was already tendered, because there was a comment in respect of it in the amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I kindly ask you to look at the Serbian version, three, four, five, six, up to the eighth, let's say here, where Karadzic says he wants to make civil war there, and then we have a cuss word. Is it true that Koprivica is telling me - and there you can see that he's the one who called me - he's telling me that he -- actually, that the Assembly president tried to get him to mobilise the Territorial Defence, and Koprivica explained: "I didn't allow that, I didn't allow it. I figured out that here he says a recommendation. Each recommendation carries a certain weight. From whom do we need to protect ourselves?" And then Karadzic says: "Whose -- he wants to make a civil war there ..." And then we have a swear word. Can we have page 2 in the English and Serbian, please, where Koprivica says: "It seems that he wants to ... distribute weapons, and if that is not allowed because the weapons are in the barracks, it is not allowed, he said, You shall create a revolt." And Karadzic says: "No way ... he wants to create -- to create a separate army, a republic army." And then a little bit lower, Koprivica informed him that he had a very good composition and that even those from the left bloc were on his side. Even though there was a Muslim from his bloc, he supported him, and the decision on the mobilisation was prevented. And then he says: "I said, You want to follow the instructions to create chaos for me, a civil war." And then Karadzic says: "And did the Serbs respond to the MUP, to the reserve police forces?" And he says: "Yes, they did. I told them to respond so that we do not stay alone, so that they do not make any sabotage." And can we look at the following page in the English and the Serbian. The next page, Koprivica says: "I said journalists cannot witness that. You are wanting to get 'pilav" according to the directives. I said, To get recommendation that carries much weight, you don't understand, I do not want to have a civil war here ..." And then Radovan Karadzic says: "That is good, excellent." So can you see, Witness, sir, that Koprivica, Rajko, and Karadzic, Radovan, are against a civil war, and that they believed that this measure was a step towards the civil war, and that Koprivica even asked Bilal, Who are we going to be fighting against in order to muster the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that we were against the civil war and that these measures we believed were leading to civil war?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What you are trying to do is twist things and facts. I am talking -- I would like to ask the Trial Chamber that the accused does not interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed to answer, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are twisting things completely. The request by the president of the Municipal Assembly is legal and legitimate. He is presiding at the Council for National Defence, and his request cannot be any kind of trick. There were valid reasons to muster the Territorial Defence units, but of course this didn't suit you, because those units that would have been mobilised would have been multi-ethnic ones, including Bosniak Muslims, Serbs, Croats, Yugoslavs, and everyone else, and this did not suit you because you already had your own Serbian Territorial Defence, you already had your weapons, and there was already enough arms that you got from the barracks that you brought to Vogosca through different JNA channels, and there was a lot of weapons also that you brought from the fronts in Croatia, because Serbs en masse took part in the fighting in Croatia. They went to Republika Srpska. They fired shots, they created troubles. So your assertion is absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like you to provide the OTP with evidence for all these assertions that you are making. What I'm asking you: Is the TO and the overall defence system in the then Yugoslavia at the time something that was subordinate to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO was not subordinated to the JNA, even though it was part of the overall All People's Defence system. It had its own civilian command, the TO had its own civilian command, but it was part of the All People's Defence system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You say that the MUP, in fact, to a large extent, became divided already on the 31st of January. Can we have a look at 65 ter 16146. The 21st of January, 1992, or the 31st. Can we have a look at this document. Can you just have a look at this document, please. Do you remember this document that you commented upon during your previous testimony as well? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have 65 ter 22107, page 12, paragraph 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out in English: [In English] "I have reviewed the document bearing the number 0063-5882 to 0063-5882." [No interpretation]: [In English] "I don't remember receiving this document, but I remember the issue. This order was issued in the times of tension, where the employees were already divided on ethnical principles. Everybody was affected at all levels." [Interpretation] And then there's a reference to the police station in Vogosca that was similarly divided. So on the 31st of January, 1992, the police was divided. Is that what you said in this statement?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which context you're referring, how it was divided. In this period, police officials --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On ethnic grounds.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Policemen worked together, both, but certainly the division was felt in the air. They worked together. They went on joint patrols, they went out on various assignments together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says "already divided." That's what it says here. Do you remember that Momcilo Mandic sent a dispatch about the establishment of two MUPs on the 31st of March, 1992, that is to say, two months after this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, your assertion is incorrect. Momcilo Mandic did send a dispatch after this date. However, it was not a dispatch on the establishment of two MUPs, and you know that very well, Mr. Accused. He sent a dispatch on the destruction of the republican MUP, on the establishment of a Serbian MUP, on taking over all employees and establishing Serb government and a Serb MUP. There was no mention of the establishment of two MUPs. That is an absolute falsehood.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call this up, 65 ter 1016.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Witness, that on the 18th of March, the Lisbon Agreement had been reached, on the basis of which the Serb entity was entitled to have its own police?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the Lisbon Agreement, but it was not verified anywhere. Tell me, where was it verified, and what made it incumbent upon me or anyone in Bosnia-Herzegovina to observe it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The consent of the top political authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The late Mr. Izetbegovic, may he rest in peace, accepted this agreement. Now, look at what Mandic says towards the bottom. Have a look at this. In English, it's also towards the bottom. All employees who were employed on the day when this document entered into force, the Security Services Centres and Public Security Stations of BH MUP on the territory of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina are abolished and cease to function, and their authority, i.e., tasks and duties within the competence of organs, and so on and so forth. And look at this: "The 27th of March, 1992, the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with the political orientation of the Serb people and the Sarajevo Agreement," and the Sarajevo Agreement is basically this Lisbon Agreement that had been reached, "promulgated the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In addition to that, the Assembly of the Serbian People passed a number of laws ..." And so on and so forth. Witness, this is based on agreement reached by the top echelons of political authority with the international community, and that was sent two months after your assertion that all of this had been divided up; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Accused, what you said here is something that is constructed. You are presenting propositions that have nothing to do with one another. The late Izetbegovic, as far as I know, did accept the Lisbon Agreement. However, the Lisbon Agreement was not verified anywhere. And I, personally, or anyone else in Bosnia-Herzegovina, were not bound by this agreement in any way. The Assembly of the Serb People that you established did not have any stronghold in the existing legislation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was an illegal creation, and all of its decisions were illegal and were actually destroying the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that includes the establishment of the Serbian MUP. The dispatch of Momo Mandic shows unequivocally that the republican MUP would no longer exist, that there would only be a Serb MUP, and that all non-Serbs have to be resubordinated and pledge their allegiance to the Serb MUP. Do you consider that to be right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you also say that it was envisaged that those Muslims who stay on in the Serb police station would go on working; however, they have to pledge allegiance, as you had put it, or, rather, be local and accept these new authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. What are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you state in your statement that you were told, from the Serb side, that those policemen who remain in the police station can stay on, on the condition that they accept this authority?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the condition that they accept an illegal, unlawful government of brigands. There were people like that as well in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and very quickly they ended up in your concentration camps. It never crossed my mind to take off some insignia and to put Serb insignia on my forehead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Everything you have to say that falls outside the scope of my question, you can say during the Prosecution's time, and then they are going to use that appropriately.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're spending my time.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're spending my time too, Mr. Accused. Allow me to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Witness. But if you can be brief, be brief as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to answer as briefly as possible. I wish to give a thorough, clear, and concrete answer to each and every one of these questions that you are putting to me. It is your problem, the fact that you don't like my answers. It's not my problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I like every answer of yours. Just make it as short as possible. When did this attack against the police station take place, the one that you described; what date? Boro Radic, you know.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. It was after this dispatch, so it was sometime in the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After the dispatch; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see what you say in your statement from 1998. 65 ter 22105, please, page 5. Paragraph 4 from the bottom. I'm going to read this in English: [In English] "After the attack on the station, Momcilo Mandic, assistant of the minister of the interior and the person in charge of criminal police at republic level, sent a written order directing that all existing police stations be split up on a national basis." [Interpretation] So after this attack; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember this particular paragraph from the statement. I know that the station was attacked after the dispatch of Momcilo Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was your memory better in 1998, better than in 2011?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Memory is a relative thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted, this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this the statement, part of which we admitted previously? No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. This is from 1998, his statement from 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1108, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. When we admit a part of a statement, let's admit it together with the first page so that we can know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not being broadcast, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Court Deputy will check it out. I don't think it was broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, who suggested to you that you should make such changes in your statements, that you change some fundamental things in your statements?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who you mean. I am a man of integrity. No one made any suggestions to me whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So it's at your own initiative that you changed these important facts in your statements; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that fact is important for you. It is for me too. But I gave the statement in 1998, so that is, what, eight years -- no, six or seven years after all of this happened. So if I made a mistake, perhaps, in terms of 10 or 15 days, I don't see any reason for that to be taken as some kind of a major mistake. After all, it's been a long time, and many things happened in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, was the possibility envisaged for Serbs, who remain in a Muslim municipality and work for a Muslim police station, also work for the police, actually?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you did not think along those lines as well. We did not think in that way in which you are thinking, Mr. Accused. For us, the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina always was, is, and shall be a multi-ethnic police force, where there is going to be room for the members of all ethnic groups. I never thought along these separatist lines as you think and your followers. I'm not interested in that kind of policy. And we never thought of eliminating the Serbs from the police, no. To this day in the federal police, in all the cantons, you have hundreds of policemen who are graduates of the Police Academy in Sarajevo, and as honest and honourable men, they conduct police work. Are they more or less Serbs than what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "We do not think that way," that's what you say. Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We Bosniak Muslims, if you want a specific and accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And we Serbs and Croats, who constitute the constitutional majority of Bosnia-Herzegovina, think along some different lines. You want to keep us in a marriage by force?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who gives you the right to speak on behalf of the Croats, and how would you know what they think? As far as I know, you don't have the right to speak in the name of the Serbs, either, any longer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's leave that aside. 30595, let's have that 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember that an offer had been made to you for you to establish a municipality, as well, consisting of the Muslim parts of the municipality. Why are you not saying that you'd get part of the urban area as well? You say that you were offered Hotonj, Gornje, Donje Ugorsko, Kobilja Glava, these villages. Why have you keep silent about the fact that you would have been given half of the city as well?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't kept silent about anything, and your claim is an absolute lie, it is totally untrue. No one offered the Bosniak Muslims any more than what I said, absolutely nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you enter these negotiations, and was that the conclusion that you reached, that nothing else had been offered to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please focus on this intercept between some Kole and Ratko Adzic, who was -- page 3 in English. I believe that that's the same in Serbian. No, it's page 5 in Serbian. Prodanovic is calling Kole. Some Prodanovic is calling Kole, Jovo Prodanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Before it disappears from the screen, I wonder if we could have a redaction at page 101, line 5. Do I have the -- 5 and 6, please. And I can explain the reason for my request in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it must be. I don't see why, but all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please direct your attention on the Serb version. It's written in Latin script, and in English it's Chapter III. Prodanovic called Kole and they have an exchange. Could we please see the following page in English. Lest I read everything, please look somewhere halfway through the page: [In English] "Well, yeah. But, hell, they didn't screw them. Don't be a fool. They wanted an Islamic state, and there's no ... they won't give up, when it's like ..." "Like," and something is illegible: "Do you think they'll make it?" "Of course." [No interpretation]: [In English] "They won't with us for sure, they can next to us ... no problem, and we shouldn't prevent them. Our dear God sent them to open our eyes, what needs to be done." [Interpretation] The text follows on the next page in Serbian, and toward the end of the English version: [In English] "Will it be divided right away?" [Interpretation] Kole responds: "It will." And then page 7 in Serbian and the following page in English, the one after this page. Prodanovic is asking questions now. His house is at Donja Vogosca, and he says: "Where will it be?" And Kole says: [In English] "It belongs to the Serbian Autonomous District of Romanija, everything from the source of the Bosna River to Visoko. Brother, all of it will be connected and incorporated into Romanija. "Of course, new municipalities will be made, a new municipality is already being made - Rajlovac, which will include Zabrdje, and the area all the way up to Vrelo Bosne and over here to the Serbian Vogosca ... Serbian Vogosca will include everything all the way to KRS... and spread down there, because the Serbs are a majority also down in the city in our local communities ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we just go over to the next page in Serbian, please, so the witness can follow along with what Dr. Karadzic is reading?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Yes, next page, please. On 7 -- we're still on page 7, but we'll soon be on page 8, and it says: [In English] "We can't take Barica from them, because that belongs to them. Barica and Kobilja Glava are theirs, and the left side is ours." And so on and so on. [Interpretation] And down there it says: "Seriously, that's better than fighting, isn't it?" Can we please see page 8 in the English. I apologise, I meant page 8 in Serbian: "Seriously, that's better than fighting, isn't it?" And he replies: "If they accept that." And so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Witness, that the Serb side agreed not to remain in Yugoslavia, under the condition that it is autonomous in Bosnia and under the condition that they establish municipalities where the Serbs are the majority?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember your assertion, but the areas you have mentioned from Vrelo Bosne to Romanija, all the way to Visoko, cannot be said to have a Serb majority. On what ground and by what right? Would you include seven-eighths of the territory of the Vogosca territory into the Serb municipality, and the Vogosca municipality has 51 per cent of Muslim population? Your allegations are ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That is not our topic, sir. That is a matter for negotiation. It's about the principle. You know about the principle, that the Serbs agreed not to remain in Yugoslavia under the condition that they received their municipalities and their entity, and the European Community accepted that. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had interest in your principles. It was your principles that brought about the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, sir. And after that, you committed the crimes you committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And why would the Serbs care for your decision to leave Yugoslavia? Why do you -- from what have you derived the right to rule our destiny?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't take you out of Yugoslavia by force. On the 1st of March, there was a referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's tomorrow. And in Bosnia, the day of independence is observed. On that day in 1992, Mr. Accused, 67 per cent of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina as splitting away from Yugoslavia. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now you want to draw me into a debate. That's not correct. 63 per cent did not vote, nor was it verified in the Assembly, nor will that day be observed tomorrow by Serbs or by Croats; only by Muslims. But you want to impose it on everybody, and that's what caused the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to answer, sir. Your Honour, may I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You don't have to ask. You are just entitled to answer any question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Bosnia-Herzegovina is a country of all the citizens living in it, including the Serbs. You can laugh, if you want. The Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But what you did, you threw it back 200 years. We had a referendum, and it was accepted by the global community, whether you like it or not. A growing number of Serbs and Croats living in the Federation observe tomorrow's holiday, and I congratulate Independence Day to you, sir, because you're still a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be tendered?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this has been already marked for identification during the testimony of Donia, which was marked for identification Exhibit P965.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 30635, is it also admitted, or, rather, is it -- does this apply to this 65 ter document also? Could we please have it displayed, 65 ter 30635, and then clarify the matter. No, it hasn't been admitted, I understand. Could we please see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a conversation of 7 March 1992. Do you remember, Witness, that as early as in mid-February, or, to be more precise, on the 20th or 22nd of February, the idea of three Bosnias had already been accepted? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that, nor would I or any Bosniak accept to have three Bosnias within Bosnia-Herzegovina. This must be a political pamphlet of yours. I don't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how many Bosnians are there now in one Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one Bosnia-Herzegovina, with two entities, with three constituent peoples. I hope you're familiar with that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see page 3 in Serbian and page 4 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, Jovan Tintor says: "Well, that's better. Let them take their part, and where it will be necessary for us to take ours, we'll take it for sure. We request nothing else that the Serbs rule those areas where -- where Serbs live, and let's Croats rule on Croatian land, and Muslims on Muslim land. Nothing else is possible." And a bit further down on page 5 in English, Tintor says -- he starts with a swear word: "... I'm even worse, believe me, if I had made such a noise, that the earth would have shaken. I talked with Seselj two nights ago and reached a decision. If it doesn't happen, I'll give Radovan an ultimatum. He was supposed to say it yesterday at the press conference." And: "You can read it today." And Zika replies: "I've read it." And Tintor says: "If they don't tighten the criteria, we won't be loyal to the Serbian Democratic Party anymore. I won't, although I am one of the founders. I will join Seselj's party that very moment, and, in fact, I am 99 per cent ... but I won't destroy this now. It's not time for that. Of course, I won't harm the Serbian cause. I can only strengthen it by joining there." He means Seselj. And Zeljko says: "We are already 80 per cent for Seselj." And then Tintor says on page 6 in English: "Brother, if that happens, I want to have you on the line, if it happens here. If they are not firm enough and if this is not solved faster, and if we fail to do this for the Serbian people, the Serbs will not stay loyal to the Serbian party. That's what I also said to Radovan, and he had to say it yesterday evening." Did you know that the Serb Democratic Party was under pressure from the ground to be more firm?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know, nor did I care. I didn't -- I wasn't interested in your internal relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And toward the bottom of the English version, the last two lines, it starts with foul language: "What the hell do we have to play up to anyone?" And so on: "They robbed us of our country ..." And it continues on the following page: "They took away my nationhood. They want me to turn -- they want to turn me into an ethnic minority. Who should I play up to? Who can do that to him?" And then foul language: "That won't happen. Here you are. Mr. President, listen to me. If necessary, please work on these preparations." So you are not interested in the political situation in the country, we are insisting on your thing, and you can see that the Serb people are upset by what's happening?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I never said I wasn't interested in the political situation of the country, and you are putting things into my mouth that I haven't said. I only said that I wasn't interested in your internal relations and your opinion regarding this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But don't you see, sir, that Mr. Tintor has the same attitude toward me as he has toward you? We are threatened, don't do that. Isn't this the same attitude toward me as it is toward you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. He looked down on me, but he was subordinate to you. He introduced himself to me as vice-president of the SDS, but it was a well-known fact that he was very arrogant and primitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way, and you shouldn't either. But can't you see him saying that he gave an ultimatum to Radovan?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with what you're putting to me. He may have acted in agreement with you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this excerpt be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. The witness didn't give any context about this intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if there's time, we can play it so you can hear it like everybody else. So what you have done for the Prosecution, you may also do for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. We admit intercepts, separate from the authenticity, when the witness is able to give some context of it. The witness said that he didn't know anything about this, these incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we see 65 ter 30638. This was also March, 11 March. 30638, has this been admitted in any way? It doesn't seem so. The Serbian version is not well legible, but Kole and Zika are talking here. Zika called Kole. I don't know who they are, but listen to what they say. Kole says: [In English] "My brother, the men must extremely careful, to the maximum, because there are those miserable bastards and scum who tend to mess things up, who want to see trouble break out. The men must be 100 per cent ready." [Interpretation] Can we see the following page. And here, toward the bottom, Ziko says: "They're working men, they are working men, and we are doing nothing." [In English] "They are working men, and we were doing nothing." [Interpretation] Let's see the following page in English. Kole says: "Well, go ahead, work." Zika says: [In English] "They're taking over the territory, part by part, and they're assuming authority, and all we do is hold Assembly sessions." [Interpretation] Kole says: [In English] "Where have they assumed authority?" [Interpretation] Zika: [In English] "Well, fuck it, have they assumed it here in Brod, they've assumed it in Travnik." [Interpretation] Kole says: [In English] "Travnik's not ours. What have we got to do with Travnik? There's Croats and Muslims there. We don't need Travnik. We need to establish authority and the Serbian state in the Serbian territory."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So that now can you see that no territories are demanded here that are not populated by a Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see that. What gave you the right to declare a territory, sir? In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the population is ethnically mixed, and there are areas where one ethnicity is dominant. But the fact that one ethnicity is less strong, in terms of numbers in a certain area, gives nobody the right to declare a territory Serb, Croat, or Bosniaks. That attitude actually brought about the consequences you inflicted on it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are now waging Communist propaganda. We wanted you to stay with us in Yugoslavia. You didn't want to. We didn't make you. But now you don't want to accept that this was our concession to you as our favour -- as the price for our leaving Yugoslavia with you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me reply to you. I've never been a member of the Communist Party. You probably were, given your position formerly. When you left it, I don't know. I've never been a member of the Communist Party. Communism, as an ideology, never enjoyed my support and I took no interest in it. The Bosniaks never considered Bosnia-Herzegovina their exclusive territory. Since the second session of the AVNOJ, Bosnia has been considered a joint entity of Bosniaks, Croats and Muslims. But since your -- on the referendum, 63 or 64 per cent of the population voted in favour of Bosnia splitting away from the truncated Yugoslavia. Or did you think that Yugoslavia was in accordance with Seselj's Chetnik ideology, everything up until the Virovitica-Karlovac-Karlobag line and cleansed of everybody but Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. In Croatia, we cleansed 160.000 Serbs from that country.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you had almost one-third of the territory of Croatia under occupation and cleansed all Croats from that territory, and there were huge Croatian victims. And now you're saying that you're big friends of theirs.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 65 ter 30650.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you threaten the garrison commander at Semizovac? You speak about that in your statement, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a very strong conversation with the commander, where he was insolent, arrogant. He humiliated me, not just me as a person, but me as a Muslim, as a member of the Muslim people. And I did tell him that if he dared to set off through Kobilja Glava, I couldn't guarantee that he would make it there alive. What he set out to do was according to your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what did you call him, and what did he call you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember who called whom what.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But actually you called him to ask him what you were doing there and what kind of exercises they were doing there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the civilian police have the right to call the army and quiz them about what they're doing?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they do. I'm responsible for law and order in the territory of my municipality, and if the barracks, where the TO weapons are held without the permission of the TO, takes out two guns with trucks and ammunition, and they fire from those guns and disturb the population, who have to seek shelter, don't I have the right to ask the responsible senior officer in the barracks what he was doing, why they were doing it, how can they do something like that without the permission of the National Defence Council, and how can they pull weapons out without permission?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that reservists, in order to join the army, need to go through training?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any police formation has a planned training programme. Reservists that you are talking about were reservists that were arriving from Croatia. These are reservists that you re-organised and re-subordinated and channeled to the Serbian Territorial Defence ranks. This is illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you deny that at that point in time, war was raging in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a well-known fact. Mr. Karadzic, I didn't say I didn't know that. It's a generally-known thing. What are you trying to say by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I feel obliged to intervene at this moment. You have spent with this witness three and a half hours, and you're still dealing with what caused the war, whose fault is it. How are these relevant to your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Excellency, joint criminal enterprise from the indictment encompasses my intentions from July 1990 and from the formation of the party. We have a witness here who was part of the joint criminal enterprise to have Bosnia split up from Yugoslavia and for Serbs to be subjugate to a single Bosnia, and you will see two attempts to throw them out of Bosnia, and you will see that this witness interfered in defence powers and matters of the Yugoslav People's Army, and this is evidence. Everything that happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina actually arose from that criminal -- joint criminal enterprise and not for the one that I am charged with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is up to you, how to efficiently use the time allotted for your cross-examination. You have an hour left. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask a question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is it, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it's an answer to one of the questions from the accused. I'm here in the capacity of a witness. No court in the world has proceedings instigated against me. There is no statement to that effect against me. There is no mention of any kind of joint criminal enterprise that I am a part of. So you are spreading untruths here, Mr. Karadzic. I did not interfere in matters of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was not a question for you. Please understand that. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at intercept of Rajko Koprivica, the president of the Executive Board of Vogosca, and General Djurdjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that General Djurdjevac was the commander of the 4th; i.e., the Sarajevo Corps of the 2nd Military District?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Vojislav Djurdjevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Rajko calls the general and says: "Things are getting complicated here in the army." And Djurdjevac says: "What?" Rajko says: "Reservists, there are several hundreds of them from Ilijas who fled from Ilijas --"

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry. Can we go in the next page in Serbian so that the witness can follow along.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Okay, then I read it in English. Rajko: "General, things are getting complicated here in the army." General: "What?" Rajko: "Reservists from -- there are several hundreds of them from Ilijas, who fled from Ilijas. They are of Muslim nationality. For us, the reserve force, they are heading towards Vogosca to take the station in Vogosca. That is the information I received from my commander." General: "I see." Rajko: "And also to take the check-points in Semizovac and that one. My men are upset, and they have organised themselves. They want to shoot at them. What are we going to do?" Djurdjevac: "And who are you?" Rajko: "I am president of the Executive Board on the Vogosca Municipality." General: "What is your last and the first name?" "Rajko Koprivica." "Oh, I see, Koprivica." Rajko: "Yes, I have visited you." [Interpretation] And Rajko says at the bottom: [In English] "Those ones from Ilijas, because Ratko is down there, practically they have split up in Ilijas. The Muslim police and now the entire reserve and the active-duty force set off towards Vogosca to take check-points and the police station." General: "The Muslim ones?" Rajko: "The Muslim ones, only the Muslim ones. It is half/half here in Vogosca." [Interpretation] And then a little bit lower, the general says: [In English] "According to the instructions on operation in the crisis situation." [Interpretation] And Rajko says: [In English] "I am afraid of the further complications. Can you help us somehow?" General: "Me, well, it won't be good if I help in any way." [Interpretation] Can we look at the following page, please, 5 in the Serbian, and the sixth, and the following page in English as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the first conversation with the general, where the general refuses to help. And then Kole is speaking with MK - this is possibly Momcilo Krajisnik - and he says: [In English] "Listen, you are a wise man. Do everything in a calm manner. Take my advice." [Interpretation] Do you remember that Krajisnik, MK -- Krajisnik -- that "MK" is Krajisnik and that "Kole" is Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the initials "MK" could stand for Momcilo Krajisnik. I don't know who Kole is, though. However, in his address -- actually, in your address, you mention two types of reservists. It's a generally-known fact, and we already discussed that today, that Bosniaks and Croats did not respond to the JNA reserve forces. The reservists who were in Ilijas were JNA reservists, and a considerable number of them came for -- they came from Croatia. And a large number of those reservists were your personnel who were thrown out from the Ilijas Police Station, and their intention was to capture the check-points in Vogosca. Actually, this is quite incorrect. There were about 30 of them. They were not a substantial military force. And on the day when the Serbs took -- occupied the local security station in Ilijas, Croats and Muslims withdrew to Srednje. You know where that is. And they remained there for four or five days, and after that, they were pushed back from the Srednje substation. Thus, there can be no talk of police reserve forces, Croats and Bosniaks, from Ilijas were going to create any kind of incident in the Vogosca municipality area. There's another important thing that you mention here, and that is some kind of instruction as to conduct during an emergency situation. What does Rajko Koprivica, the president of the Executive Board of the Vogosca Municipality, have anything to do with General Vojislav Djurdjevac, who is the commander of some military district, for this one to be issuing him some kind of instruction as to how to behave in some kind of emergency situation? This would indicate that you had already -- had a worked-out scenario of taking power, and how you would ethnically cleanse Ilijas and Vogosca and all the other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to notice here that Krajisnik says: "God forbid that anyone is killed." Can you please look at that. This is page 6 in the Serbian: "God forbid that anybody should get killed. You are a wise man. You should do everything in a calm manner." I don't need to read that whole thing. Can we look at page 7 in the Serbian and then page 8 in the Serbian. The English page is all right. You can see that Krajisnik is trying to calm things down: "You are wise. You should try to preserve peace at all costs." And then he asks: "On what grounds did you call Commander Crnogorac and threaten him, even though you're a civilian and he's a military officer?"

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would briefly like to call up P2359 of the 4th of April, 1992. This is the day before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The day before the war broke out, Momcilo Krajisnik and Jovan Tintor are speaking, and Krajisnik says: "Where are you calling from?" Tintor says: "From the HQ." And Tintor says: "I hear you've been informed. Rajko has told me about that part. They are getting ready up there. Reportedly, they are on the move already." Krajisnik: "Who's on the move?" Tintor: "Well, the Muslims from Kobilja Glava." Krajisnik: "Yeah." Tintor: "They are on their way towards Grahoviste, towards Zuc, and the situation is very intense. I think a conflict will break out up there." Can we go to the following page both in B/C/S and in English, please. Krajisnik says: "Look, I've just spoken with Rajko." Tintor: "Yes." "I told him to inform this Momo Mandic for the police, you know." "Yes." Krajisnik says: "Best man, we need to try everything to calm the situation down." Tintor: "Yes, Momo Mandic has been on the spot." Krajisnik: "That's the most important thing finally. The people do need to organise themselves, but under no circumstances should we look for trouble. It is very important to keep peace, you know." "Yes." But can you see how much effort the Serbian effort put in from the very top? Krajisnik was the president of the Assembly to keep the peace.

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on what I've been through and what I've experienced, I really cannot agree with your assertion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document has already been admitted, so we will not tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You called this commander, Crnogorac, and then Djurdjevac. The general called you, personally. This is described in paragraph 67 from your statement from 2007, where you say that he asked you why -- he says: "An hour after that, General Djurdjevac called me personally. He was Crnogorac's commander. He asked me, why did I threaten his commander in Semizovac. I answered that I would have threatened him, too, had he been doing the same thing that Crnogorac was doing. I also told him that I don't consider the JNA to be my army anymore. He called me an anti-Yugoslav and a Mujahedin, and said that he would very quickly have to start dealing with us." And so on and so forth. Thus, you interfered in the defence preparations of the Yugoslav People's Army, which at the time was the only legitimate military force in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree with you on all issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, you didn't interfere, or it wasn't legitimate?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not interfere. And the weapons that we are talking about were the weapons of the Territorial Defence, so it wasn't the weapons of the JNA that we're talking about. The JNA most probably at that point in time was still a legitimate military power in Bosnia and Herzegovina, for another two weeks, perhaps, after that, but none of the Bosniaks or the Croats considered them as their own. They believed it to be the Serbo-Chetnik army, which ultimately that's exactly what it turned out to be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 71 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, please. If it is not in this form in the amalgamated statement, I'd like to tender paragraph 67 and also 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out to you now: "I had information that Rajko Koprivica, Momo Krajisnik, Tintor and Mirko Krajisnik were meeting at [indiscernible], Kotonje." Kotonje was a town with a majority Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't a Muslim majority. There's quite a few Serbs there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I continue: "Mirko Krajisnik also did business with Tintor in Vogosca. I saw that group, including Krajisnik, once or twice. One of the waiters there was one of my informants. He was a Serb, because not a single Muslim could be employed there." So you are saying that Krajisnik and Tintor were best men at each other's weddings? And you say that -- and you said that you did not have the right to have the president of the Parliament followed, but now we see that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have construed all of this, and it's not true. I am not aware of the fact that these two gentlemen were best men at each other's weddings, nor do I know anything about that. That Krajisnik and Tintor were involved in smuggling and things like that is a generally-known fact. It is true that I had a man working there who sent information to me, yes, that's no secret, and I stated that, yes, he was a Serb, but he reported to me personally, saying what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you not say here that they were involved in smuggling? You say that they were involved in business. Do you have any kind of judgement stating that they were smugglers?

utterances.speaker: KDZ020 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not for Mirko Krajisnik, but for Momcilo Krajisnik and you, yes. The two of you were found guilty of crime, and you were convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I was acquitted as well, sir. Don't you know that? And all of that is slander, and it's part of our political life, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be it for today. We'll adjourn. But I wanted to put it on the record I would like to thank the Trial Chamber in the Tolimir case, which has kindly moved its hearing to Courtroom II so that we could have an extended sitting today. Tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
